overview.title: TRM UI
overview.sub: The design system and component library behind Turing Mirror desktop products
overview.whatBody:
A set of design tokens, a component library, eight-language i18n, and a build setup that runs as-is.
Extracted from RVC Fabric, but it depends on no product code — the whole src/trm/ directory can be copied out.
overview.whyBody:
“Copy RVC Fabric’s UI” kept turning into “fork the whole repository and hack on it”, so every new product started from a pile of code it never needed, and the design system was kept in sync by hand — drifting a little further with every pass.
Pulling the interface layer out on its own means new products start here, and improvements flow back here — instead of into five diverging copies.
overview.rule1: Every colour comes from a token. A hard-coded colour is guaranteed wrong in the other theme — and only visible when someone switches.
overview.rule2: Every string comes from a locale pack. All eight are forced into the same shape by a build-time check, not by good intentions.
overview.rule3: src/trm/ imports nothing outside itself. The moment it reaches into product code, the template degrades into “part of one product”.
overview.themeTip: “Follow system” writes no data-theme and relies on prefers-color-scheme; picking light or dark stamps the attribute onto <html>.
overview.langTip: All eight packs are bundled at build time, so switching is a synchronous swap — no flash of raw keys before the text arrives.

components.sub: Everything below is a live control, not a screenshot.
components.buttonsNote: A busy button must not just go grey: grey is a state, the moving dots are the receipt. Without them, “working” and “didn’t register my click” look identical.
components.segmentNote: One thumb that slides, not a separate background painted under each button. The difference is “the same object moved” versus “this one went out and that one came on” — the latter is two flickers.

field.name: Display name
field.nameTip: The help mark has to be a button that swallows its own click — it often sits inside a label, and a label forwards clicks to the control it owns.
field.deviceDesc: A saved option that has left the list stays visible and says so — rendering an empty box would pretend it was never set.
field.volumeNote: While dragging, the knob is drawn at the pointer’s real position with no transition; it glides onto the step only when you let go — and that snap is what tells you which step you actually got.

list.item1Body:
“Looks clickable” and “is clickable” have to agree. This row once had only the styling; no onClick was ever wired. People clicked it four times, nothing happened, and they concluded the app was broken.

Now the styling follows whether an onClick exists — not a separate clickable flag.
list.item2: Anything can go on the right

type.sub: Body is 15px at 1.65 line-height. The size steps are fixed — don’t slip a new value in between them.
type.sample: Schale’s light blue, brought over to desktop software.

color.sub: Switch to dark and look again: every swatch has to hold up in both themes.

motion.sub: Page direction follows the nav order. Click a few tabs above and you’ll see it.
motion.easeNav: Page transitions only. Fast off the mark, long on the tail, and it never overshoots — the page layer sits flush with the window edge, and an overshoot is a visible seam.
motion.spring: For small elements. It overshoots, so it only goes on things that don’t touch the window edge — the segment thumb, floating panels.
motion.ease: The general-purpose transition. Hover, press, colour changes.
motion.reduce: If the system asks for reduced motion, all of the above switches off. That is not optional — large sliding animations make people with vestibular sensitivity dizzy.
